Timeline::epoch_nanos¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Series Timeline::epoch_nanos() const

What It Does¶

epoch_nanos() exposes the timeline’s machine-time values as an Int64 Series while preserving the timeline’s logical shape. It is the bridge to numeric operations: masks, reshaping, serialization utilities, exact differences, and custom computations that naturally operate on Series.

Unlike ticks(), this method does not flatten a matrix or 3-D temporal array into a C++ vector. Unlike host(), it returns one stable result type regardless of rank and cardinality.

The values are UTC epoch nanoseconds. The timeline’s presentation timezone is not embedded in the numeric Series; retain tz() separately if the values will later be reconstructed with the same wall-clock presentation.

The result is newly materialized rather than a mutable view into the Timeline. Numeric transformations of the returned Series do not rewrite the source timeline.

Returns¶

An Int64 Series with the same shape and number of positions as the source timeline. Absent instants appear as Timeline::kNaT.

Examples¶

Example 1. Preserve matrix shape while exposing exact ticks.

auto matrix = pluss::timeline::make({
    {"2024-02-29T12:30:00Z", "2024-03-01T00:00:00Z"},
    {"2024-03-02T06:15:00Z", ""},
});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, matrix.epoch_nanos());
std::cout << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 1709209800000000000  1709251200000000000 ⎤
⎣ 1709360100000000000 -9223372036854775808 ⎦

Example 2. Compare shape-preserving and flattening exports.

auto matrix = pluss::timeline::epoch({2, 3});
auto series = matrix.epoch_nanos();
auto vector = matrix.ticks();

std::cout << "series dim=" << series.dim()
          << ", series numel=" << series.numel()
          << ", vector size=" << vector.size() << "\n";

Output¶

series dim=2, series numel=6, vector size=6

Example 3. Build a validity mask without mistaking the NaT sentinel for an ordinary early date.

auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-02-29T12:30:00Z", "", "2024-03-01T00:00:00Z"
});
auto valid = times.epoch_nanos().ne(pluss::Timeline::kNaT);
pluss::series::print(std::cout, valid);
std::cout << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false, true]

For ordinary validity work, isvalid() communicates this intent more directly. The numeric form is useful when a larger numeric pipeline already operates on epoch ticks.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The returned Series contains no timezone metadata. Save tz() separately for a presentation-preserving round trip.

  • Arithmetic on raw epoch values is integer arithmetic. Prefer Timeline and Duration methods when calendar or absent-instant semantics matter.

  • Never treat Timeline::kNaT as an ordinary timestamp; filter or mask it before ordering or arithmetic in a generic numeric pipeline.

  • This method preserves shape; call flatten() explicitly if a flat Series is required.

  • The conversion allocates an independent Series; cache it if several downstream numeric operations will reuse the same ticks.

Summary¶

Use epoch_nanos() for a shape-preserving numeric bridge, the vector methods for owning flat C++ data, and host() when a rank-sensitive host variant is the desired integration format.
